'''''Coriaria nepalensis''''' is a [[shrub]] of the genus ''[[Coriaria]]''. It grows in the foothills of the [[Himalayas]]. It blooms in spring and has bright yellow flowers and red fruits in summer.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/8600020?projectid=32|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden|title=Coriaria nepalensis Wall.|author=Tropicos.org|accessdate=10 February 2013}}</ref>

The plant is also known in English as '''masuri berry''', '''tanner's tree''', or '''mansur shrub'''. In [[Hindi language|Hindi]] it is known as masuri ({{lang|hi|मसूरी}}), makola, or masurya ({{lang|hi|मसूरिया}}); and in [[Nepali language|Nepali]] as macchaino ({{lang|ne|मछाईनो}}).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Masuri%20Berry.html|work=Flowers of India|title=Coriaria nepalensis|accessdate=22 February 2013}}</ref>

==Description==
''C. nepalensis'' is a shrub, growing around 1.5-2.5 metres tall. Flowers, yellow in colour, are in groups ([[inflorescence]]s) and they are male or female but in the same plant. It blooms from February to May.<ref name="coriaria" />

Fruits are red to dark purple when mature. They resemble [[berry (botany)|berries]], but they are actually [[achene]]s protected by enlarged and colored petals. The fruits are produced from May to August, but they are inedible as their seeds are poisonous.<ref name="coriaria" />

The number of [[chromosome]]s the plant has is 40.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Yokoyama, J. |author2=Suzuki M. |author3=Iwatsuki K. |author4=Hasebe M. |name-list-style=amp |title=Molecular phylogeny of Coriaria, with special emphasis on the disjunct distribution. |year=2000 |journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=11–19 |doi= 10.1006/mpev.1999.0672 |pmid=10631039|bibcode=2000MolPE..14...11Y }}</ref>

''C. nepalensis'' is toxic due to the presence of [[coriamyrtin]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.toxicon.2005.06.026 | title = Poisoning by Coriaria myrtifolia Linnaeus: A new case report and review of the literature | date = 2005 | last1 = De Haro | first1 = Luc | last2 = Pommier | first2 = Philip | last3 = Tichadou | first3 = Lucia | last4 = Hayek-Lanthois | first4 = Maryvonne | last5 = Arditti | first5 = Jocelyne | journal = Toxicon | volume = 46 | issue = 6 | pages = 600–603 | pmid = 16165183 | bibcode = 2005Txcn...46..600D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1080/15563650.2020.1832677 | title = Sweet poison: Seizures in two patients with ''Coriaria intermedia'' poisoning | date = 2021 | last1 = Chen | first1 = Yen-Chin | last2 = Chen | first2 = Hsien-Yi | last3 = Huang | first3 = Li-Chi | last4 = Yu | first4 = Jiun-Hao | journal = Clinical Toxicology | volume = 59 | issue = 6 | pages = 533–534 | pmid = 33112689 }}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''C. nepalensis'' grows on the southern slopes of the [[Himalayas]] (in [[Bhutan]], [[India]], [[Nepal]], [[Pakistan]]), usually between 800 and 2500 metres.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=200012674|title=Coriaria nepalensis|work=Flora of Pakistan|author=Abdul Ghafoor|accessdate=2013-02-10}}</ref>

This species was also found in southern [[China]] in mountain slopes at 200–3200 m high. It has been found in the Chinese provinces of [[Gansu]], [[Guangxi]], [[Guizhou]], [[Henan]], [[Hong Kong]], [[Hubei]], [[Hunan]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Shaanxi]], [[Sichuan]], [[Xizang]], and [[Yunnan]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012674|title=Coriaria nepalensis|work=Flora of China|author1=Tien-lu Ming |author2=Anthony R. Brach |accessdate=2013-02-10}}</ref>
